searchText: **ChrisLinn** (in reply to **vbuterin**) also need to deal with sybil attacks 1 person pretending 1000+ (or the majority) **vbuterin** It's not a 51% thing, only need one of the participants to be trustworthy **vbuterin** So hopefully everyone in this room would participate and publish that fact for example My biggest fear with trusted setups is that the cryptography is complicated and there are like 5 people in the world whowgrok it enough to actually validate the source code, and if we are lucky two of them will actually look at the source code, and the chances that they find/recognize bugs is low. It is my problem with Tornado.cash's trusted setup for example, I'm not confident that more than one person has actually validated the code for it. And by validated I mean actually sat down and audited it themselves, looking for exploits in the cryptography or neighboring concepts. I looked at the code and have no idea if it is correct or not, for example. And when I asked other auditors if it was sound they basically said "it looks right I guess?" Isn't this a common issue among *all* trusted cryptography that we mitigate via paying for reviews from professionals? Yes, but at least with ECDSA it is well established with a long history and a lot of review. Same with hashing algorithms. I feel like both are used *way* more broadly by humanity and you can easily find a library to compare results against, and the library doesn't have to be tightly integrated with the project and have custom code around it. In most of cryptography there is just a single pure function, and you can find dozens of battle tested implementations to compare results against. With zkProofs and trusted setups, the cryptography has to be woven much more tightly into your code. Plus the set of cryptographers who understand it is smaller as well. I have implemented my own keccak256 and secp256k1 libraries, but I have no clue how zkProofs and trusted setup works (as an anecdotal example). Sure, the crypto is complex. But we can actually ensure people look at the code (by paying them) and we certainly shouldn't settle for any review that equates to "looks right i guess". If you're only willing to trust crypto with ECDSA history then I think you're going to feel uncomfortable with BLS too. We need to push boundaries with crypto at *some point*, so I think we should be careful with impeding innovation by just declaring it impossible to be analyzed just because *some* projects have failed to get a proper analysis. I can appreciate that argument. Basically my argument boils down to, "how much does a trusted setup help us with design, and is that worth the risks it introduces of using novel cryptography?" If it is just, "we can save a couple bytes on the wire" then it isn't worth it. If it is, "we have no other solution to a hard problem that we must solve" then I'm ok with it. Agreed 🙂 **mikerah** (in reply to **<@301186049323958275>**) Another issue with trusted setup that often doesn't appear is the social factor. All you need is a well-resource nefarious actor to get most people to believe they can provide all the necessary components of a trusted setup and have people blindly trust them. **mikerah** Of course, I think most of this is mitigated with the use of universal and updated ZKPs where you have 1 trusted setup for all relevant circuits **HAOYUatHZ** isn't it the case that ligeroinc + https://notes.ethereum.org/@JustinDrake/HJhHGOljB + https://github.com/ligeroinc/LigeroRSA + https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/374.pdf and semaphore + https://github.com/appliedzkp/semaphore-phase2-setup/ + https://hackmd.io/oja21FipQ5KhQcXeyuQWFQ already have similar experiences on trusted setup? What about asking them if there is anything we need to be careful with? **vbuterin** <@301186049323958275> so in the case of the PLONK trusted setup, I personally wrote a python implementation and participated with it **vbuterin** So we know there's at least two implementations Two is certainly better than 1! **vbuterin** Actually, the *math* behind trusted setups is quite easy, at least on top of a base of assuming elliptic curve cryptography and pairings **vbuterin** But then eth2 is using BLS anyway, so we can't avoid the latter Ideally, for something as critical as Ethereum, I would like to see 3-5 independent implementations with 2-3 of them public (and easy to use by anyone) and the remaining private (security by obscurity). **vbuterin** yep, I agree! **vbuterin** One reason why I think a 2**24 size is better is precisely that it makes it easier to make an implementation **vbuterin** no need to optimize
